name: Push-Up
instructions:
## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. Your elbows should be stacked under your shoulders with your arms pointing straight down toward the ground.
    2. For comfort, you optionally can set up on an exercise mat.
2. Situate your hands mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other, with your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other.
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon which hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
3. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the ground.
    1. Let your elbows flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This commonly results in the upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of the push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, remaining shoulder-width the whole rep, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This classic exercise primarily trains your [pec major](https://www.notion.so/Pectoralis-Major-1b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728?pvs=21), which is assisted by your [front delts](https://www.notion.so/Deltoid-Anterior-Head-1905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4?pvs=21), [triceps](https://www.notion.so/Triceps-Brachii-1b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c?pvs=21), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

name: Placeholder Chest Press
instructions:
## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneously brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    2. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Once the bar contacts your chest, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This time-tested exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](https://www.notion.so/Pectoralis-Major-1b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728?pvs=21) while also training your [front delts](https://www.notion.so/Deltoid-Anterior-Head-1905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4?pvs=21) and [triceps](https://www.notion.so/Triceps-Brachii-1b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c?pvs=21).

name: Placeholder Lat Pulldown
instructions:
## Setting up
1. Connect a lat pulldown bar to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. If you do not have a standard lat pulldown bar attachment, which has a straight body and mildly angled ends, you can use a different attachment that lets you comfortably grasp it with an underhand grip.
2. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a closer than shoulder-width underhand grip, such that your palms face backward.
    1. Specifically how closely you position your hands is up to your preference, but they should be clearly closer than what you would use for a standard [underhand grip lat pulldown](Underhand%20grip%20cable%20lat%20pulldown%201a15c6f170d880b2a97ec3d948120f99.md) with a moderate grip width.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
3. While holding the bar, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
4. In the seated position, slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    2. From this position, your elbows should be straight, with your arms overhead and slightly forward (rather than completely vertical), and you should feel tension from the cable station holding your arms in this position.
    3. If you notice the cable remains slack in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), widening out your grip may be needed to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down toward your sides as you progressively bend them.
    1. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. After the initial half of the pull, when your upper arms are approximately parallel with the ground, the bony prominence on the back of each elbow should be pointing predominantly forward as your upper arms are situated in front of your body, rather than having your elbows and upper arms predominantly flared out to your sides.
    3. During the second half of this pull, drive your elbows simultaneously backward and downward until they are in line with your torso or slightly behind it.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the bar in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](https://www.notion.so/Latissimus-Dorsi-1905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47?pvs=21), [teres major](https://www.notion.so/Teres-Major-1905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6?pvs=21), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](https://www.notion.so/Biceps-Brachii-1b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68?pvs=21), [brachialis](https://www.notion.so/Brachialis-18f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9?pvs=21), and [brachioradialis](https://www.notion.so/Brachioradialis-1905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3?pvs=21).

name: Placeholder Curl
instructions:
## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, clip in a straight bar attachment and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with extended elbows.
3. Grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder width grip and an underhand grip such that your palms are directed forward.
4. While keeping your elbows extended, stand upright while gripping the bar.
5. Make sure tension is present from the cable station while your elbows are fully extended, rather than slack being present in the cable.
    1. Depending on your arm length relative to your height and which specific cable station you are using, you likely will have to take a small step backward to take out the slack of the cable.
    2. When taking a small step backward, the cable will now have a mildly diagonal line of pull rather than being vertical.
    3. To maintain a fully extended elbow position with a diagonal line of pull, you will position your upper arms slightly in front of your body by flexing at your shoulders instead of keeping your upper arms pinned to your sides (like you would with a curl that has a vertically directed resistance, such as free weights).
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the bar upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed in the same position that allowed your elbows to be fully extended at the start of the rep (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing further forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms in the same position used to start the rep.
3. Alternate between curling the bar upwards and lowering it down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](https://www.notion.so/Biceps-Brachii-1b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68?pvs=21), [brachialis](https://www.notion.so/Brachialis-18f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9?pvs=21), and [brachioradialis](https://www.notion.so/Brachioradialis-1905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3?pvs=21).

name: Placeholder Row
instructions:
## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees) and set a pair of dumbbells under the head of the bench.
    1. You can alternatively set your bench at a moderate incline (e.g., near 45 degrees) if your bench lacks a low incline setting, or if you personally prefer to use a mildly greater incline.
    2. The dumbbells may be easiest to grasp while lying on the bench if you initially place one end of each dumbbell on top of the bench’s horizontal base leg (which is where wheels may be located) and the other end of each dumbbell on the floor closer to where you will be on the bench.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
3. Grasp one dumbbell at a time, position your arms so that they are perpendicular to the ground with extended elbows, and direct your palms backward to utilize an overhand grip.
    1. The bony bump on the back of each elbow should point directly out to the side (which is the direction you will row), rather than pointing backward.
    2. To be able to row through a full range of motion, the dumbbells should not be in contact with the ground or the base of the bench, which may be more challenging to avoid for individuals with longer arms.
    3. To create greater clearance between the dumbbells and the ground, you can scoot further up toward the head of the bench.
    4. If it is difficult for you to grasp the dumbbells, which may be more likely if you have shorter arms, you can initially place the dumbbells closer to the bench’s seat before setting up with your torso scooted further down on the bench to situate your hands closer to the floor. After grasping the dumbbells, you can then press your feet into the ground to scoot further up on the bench so that your head can hang off the bench rather than having your face pressed into the head of the bench.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows straight out to your sides and upward in an arcing motion to row the dumbbells up. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. To focus on your upper back, emphasize flaring your elbows straight out from your sides so your upper arms and torso form a “T-shape” at the top of the row. 
    2. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being approximately level with your shoulders at the end of the lifting phase.
    3. Keep your palms facing backward and torso in contact with the chest pad throughout the set.
    4. When allowing your elbows to bend naturally, your forearms should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    5. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells inward in a controlled arcing motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart and forward to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Avoid tucking your elbows back toward your sides to keep the emphasis on your upper back.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights pull your arms down rapidly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to place the dumbbells back onto the ground.
## Description
This row can effectively develop your [traps](https://www.notion.so/Trapezius-1b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f?pvs=21), [rhomboids](https://www.notion.so/Rhomboids-1b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509?pvs=21), and [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also training your [biceps](https://www.notion.so/Biceps-Brachii-1b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68?pvs=21), [brachialis](https://www.notion.so/Brachialis-18f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9?pvs=21), [brachioradialis](https://www.notion.so/Brachioradialis-1905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3?pvs=21), and three [rotator cuff](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md) muscles.

name: Placeholder Hip Thrust
instructions:
## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails), and position the bar somewhat below knee height with the safety hooks resting on the safety bars.
    1. The proper starting height of the bar should comfortably allow you to get into the starting position. If the bar is too low, it can be difficult initially to move your hips under the bar with a bench behind you. If the bar is too high, you will be unable to lift your hips high enough to receive the bar initially without arching your back excessively.
2. Determine whether your Smith machine has angled or purely vertical sliding rails.
    1. If your machine has angled sliding rails, it will be ideal for you to position your bench (or other object during the next step) on the side that allows the bar to track slightly forward when lifting the bar up and slightly backward when lowering it. This means that the bottom of the rails should be horizontally closer to the bench than the top of the rails. However, the direction in which the rails angle can vary among different machines, and you may be restricted from setting up on a bench on the side of the machine’s frame. You can still hip thrust with the bar tracking backward during the lifting phase, but it may not feel as natural compared to if the bar tracks forward while lifting up.
    2. If your machine has angled sliding rails, it does not matter which side you face during this exercise.
3. Situate a flat exercise (or viable alternative) in front of the bar with the length of the bench parallel to the length of the bar.
    1. Position the bench at a distance from the bar that specifically enables you to rest your upper back comfortably on the edge of the bench while the bar is on the crease of your hips. Finding this position may require some trial and error, which is why it is recommended to perform a couple of hip thrust reps with the empty bar before you add weight plates.
    2. A specific hip thrust bench is ideal to use if you can move it, but it is not commonly available.
    3. If you use a mobile exercise bench, make sure that it will not slide back during the exercise. In contrast to a barbell hip thrust, it is not normally feasible to anchor a bench against a rack or wall when using an immobile Smith machine. However, you can place some heavy weight plates against the back of your bench if you are concerned it may slide back during your set. Note that certain benches may be more likely to slide than others.
    4. You may also be able to use a soft plyometric box near knee height that is anchored in the same manner as a flat bench.
    5. What ultimately matters is selecting an object that is sturdy, stable, and reasonably close to being knee height while being comfortable enough to support your upper back.
4. Optionally, obtain a pad (or an object that can function as a pad) that you will place between the bar and your hips.
    1. Using a pad is not required but strongly recommended because it can be very uncomfortable to have a barbell directly resting on your hip bones with a meaningful load.
    2. You can wrap a hip thrust pad or a squat pad around the middle of the bar.
    3. Alternatively, you can place a thick foam or folded exercise mat on the crease of your hip during the next step and subsequently keep it there to cushion your hip bones. Be aware that foam pads not specifically designed for hip thrusts may be somewhat damaged from this exercise.
5. Sit down on the ground with your upper back against the edge of the bench and your legs straight out in front of you under the bar.
    1. Specifically place the lower part of your shoulder blades against the edge of the bench. Feel free to adjust your upper back positioning mildly from this point based on what feels most stable to you.
    2. The middle of the bar should be aligned with the midline of your body.
6. Bring your heels toward your buttocks by bending your knees mildly greater than 90 degrees, with the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. It is normally appropriate to position your feet far enough back that your knees will be bent by approximately 90 degrees at the top of your hip thrust. From this placement, you can adjust specifically where you situate your feet based on your preference.
7. Grasp the bar with your palms facing down, and tuck your chin mildly toward your chest.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than your hips, you can adjust your grip width based on what feels stable and comfortable to you during this exercise.
    2. Continue holding the bar and keeping your chin mildly tucked throughout the exercise.
8. Using the form described in the exercise technique section, perform a couple of hip thrust reps with the empty bar to confirm that your bench placement lets the bar comfortably rest on the crease of your hips.
    1. If the bar is not positioned appropriately relative to your hips, adjust your bench placement prior to checking again until you have determined that you are set up correctly.
    2. Positioning the bar appropriately will help you avoid the excessive discomfort that may arise from positioning the bar too high (i.e., directly on your lower abdomen) or too low (i.e., directly on your groin).
    3. Some people may experience discomfort when the bar looks aligned with the crease of their hips if the bar is directly resting on the bony bumps on the front of their hip bones. If you notice that this occurs for you, you can move the bench slightly further back away from the bar to shift the pressure away from these bony bumps.
9. Load the bar with your intended weight, and assume the starting position by repeating steps 5-7.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should either be flat or exhibit its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
2. Lift your hips up until the bar is fully resting on the crease of your hips and the safety hooks are no longer resting on the safety bars.
    1. By keeping both feet on the ground, you can initially use your right and left glutes to unrack the weight.
3. Rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
4. Squeeze your glutes to continue lifting up until you can draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side.
    1. Since the bar begins from an elevated position, you may not have to lift your hips up much further from when you initially received the bar to reach this position.
5. Shift your weight into one foot on the ground, and lift the other foot off the ground. Keep one foot off the ground while hip thrusting with your other side.
    1. Based on your preference, you can lift your one leg up with a straight knee or a bent knee. Either position for the free leg is viable, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging compared to keeping it bent.
    2. So long as you lift the free leg high enough to keep its foot off the ground throughout the set, you can decide how high you lift it up.
    3. During the set, keep your right and left hip bones level with each other as you avoid letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg tilt down. You can imagine balancing a mug of water on the middle of your waist. If laser beams were shooting out from the center of your chest and your imaginary belt buckle, the two lasers should be parallel to each other throughout your set.
6. Lower your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your machine permits.
    1. With most Smith machines, the depth to which you can lower your hips will be determined by when the bar reaches the bottom of the slide rails. These Smith machines reach their lowest position before the weight plates or your buttocks can contact the ground, resulting in a shorter range of motion than a barbell hip thrust. If you are using one of these machines, you can tap the bar lightly against the bottom of the machine.
    2. Certain Smith machines permit you to lower the bar through the same range as if you used a barbell. With one of these less common machines, you can finish the lowering phase when either the weight plates lightly contact the ground, or you have reached the end range your hip mobility comfortably permits.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull the bar down abruptly, as opposed to you using your glutes to control the descent actively. Do not bounce the bar out of the bottom position.
7. Lift your hips up by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your working leg’s knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving at your hip and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise.
    4. Throughout the exercise, the sole of your working side’s foot should remain fully planted on the ground, and your upper back should remain firmly in contact with the bench.
    5. Continue holding the bar for stability, but avoid trying to lift the bar up or push it down with your hands.
8. Alternate between steps 6 and 7 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. For tracking purposes, each rep finishes after you have fully lifted your hips from the bottom position. The initial movement you performed during step 4 does not constitute a full rep.
9. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, return your previously elevated foot to the ground before shifting your weight into that side, lifting your opposite foot off the ground, and performing a set with your other side.
10. Once you have finished the lifting phase of your last rep, rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars, and lower your hips until the safety hooks are fully resting on the safety bars.
## Description
This exercise will predominantly develop your [gluteus maximus](https://www.notion.so/Gluteus-Maximus-1bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f?pvs=21) while also training your [quads](https://www.notion.so/1be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d?pvs=21) to a lesser degree.
